title: Judges 8:22–28
context: Judges 8:22–28 records the aftermath of the victory. The men of Israel offer Gideon hereditary rule, and he refuses, declaring, “The LORD shall rule over you.” Yet he asks for the gold earrings from the plunder and makes an ephod, which he places in his town of Ophrah. The narrator’s verdict is direct: “all Israel played the prostitute with it there; and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house.” The section closes with the land at rest for forty years. Both traditions read Gideon’s refusal of kingship as a right confession of the LORD’s rule, and both take seriously the narrator’s judgment on the ephod.

verses.text: Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, “Rule over us, both you, your son, and your son’s son also; for you have saved us out of the hand of Midian.”
verses.arminianNotes: The men of Israel say, “Rule over us … for you have saved us out of the hand of Midian.” Arminian readers note that the people credit Gideon with their deliverance, forgetting the lesson of 7:2 that God reduced the army precisely so Israel would not say “My own hand has saved me.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the offer of dynastic rule (“you, your son, and your son’s son also”) amounts to a request for kingship, and that it misplaces credit for salvation. Shared ground: both traditions read the offer as a failure to recognize that the LORD was Israel’s deliverer, setting up Gideon’s reply in 8:23.

verses.text: Gideon said to them, “I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you. The LORD shall rule over you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon answers, “I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you. The LORD shall rule over you.” Arminian readers see a right confession: Israel’s true King is the LORD. Gideon’s words affirm that human leadership must remain under God’s rule, a principle Samuel later echoes (1 Samuel 12:12).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the confession of the LORD’s kingship as central to Israel’s covenant identity; later the LORD tells Samuel that the people “have rejected me as the king over them” (1 Samuel 8:7). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an affirmation of God’s reign, while noting that Gideon’s later actions (8:24–31) do not fully match his words.

verses.text: Gideon said to them, “I do have a request: that you would each give me the earrings of his plunder.” (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.)
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon asks for the earrings of the plunder, “For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.” Arminian readers note the turn from refusal to request. Gideon declines a crown but accepts gold, and the request seems modest in the moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the request recalls Aaron’s call for golden rings to make the calf (Exodus 32:2). The term Ishmaelites overlaps with Midianites elsewhere (compare Genesis 37:25, 28). Shared ground: both traditions read the request as an ominous turn, preparing for the narrator’s verdict on the ephod in 8:27.

verses.text: They answered, “We will willingly give them.” They spread a garment, and every man threw the earrings of his plunder into it.
verses.arminianNotes: The people answer, “We will willingly give them,” and throw the earrings onto a spread garment. Arminian readers note the people’s generosity toward their deliverer, a sign of their gratitude and of Gideon’s standing among them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the eagerness of the response, which again parallels the giving of gold in Exodus 32:3. Generosity directed wrongly can lead to harm. Shared ground: both traditions read the scene as showing the people’s gratitude, and both read it in light of how the gold will be used.

verses.text: The weight of the golden earrings that he requested was one thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold, in addition to the crescents, and the pendants, and the purple clothing that was on the kings of Midian, and in addition to the chains that were about their camels’ necks.
verses.arminianNotes: The earrings weigh “one thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold,” beside crescents, pendants, royal purple and camel chains. A shekel is about 10 grams, so 1700 shekels is about 17 kilograms (about 37.4 pounds). Arminian readers note the great wealth gathered, which itself becomes a temptation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the royal trappings, crescents and purple, surround Gideon with the symbols of the kingship he refused. Deuteronomy 17:17 warns Israel’s king not to “greatly multiply to himself silver and gold.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing how wealth and status accumulated around Gideon, preparing for the snare of 8:27.

verses.text: Gideon made an ephod out of it, and put it in Ophrah, his city. Then all Israel played the prostitute with it there; and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon makes an ephod and places it in Ophrah, and “all Israel played the prostitute with it there; and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house.” The text does not state Gideon’s intention. Arminian readers note that even a sincere leader can set up something that leads others astray, and that the narrator’s verdict is clear and severe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that an ephod was a priestly garment (Exodus 28:6), and its use outside God’s appointed worship led to idolatry, as with Micah’s ephod later (17:5). The word “snare” echoes 2:3, “their gods will be a snare to you.” Shared ground: both traditions take the narrator’s judgment at face value and read the verse as a warning about worship devised by human initiative.

verses.text: So Midian was subdued before the children of Israel, and they lifted up their heads no more. The land had rest forty years in the days of Gideon.
verses.arminianNotes: Midian is subdued, “and they lifted up their heads no more. The land had rest forty years in the days of Gideon.” Arminian readers note that God’s deliverance brings real rest, a sign of his mercy even though Gideon’s ephod already threatens Israel’s faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the rest comes from God, who remains faithful to his people despite the failures of their leaders. The forty years recall the rest under Othniel (3:11). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a summary of God’s gracious deliverance, while the following verses show how fragile Israel’s faithfulness remained.
